It should be noted that our proposal finds common ground with prior work on public value and innovation, such as Prainsack's notions of data justice and solidarity in the realm of data governance. 76 This can introduce new incentives beyond profitability, thereby encouraging companies to change how they design and deploy new technologies. It likewise provides additional leverage to regulators and the judiciary to demand changes when harmful subsidized products are placed on the market (see below).

Policymakers and regulators have a legal mandate to balance competing interests ( §4 ). The vague promise that AI products and services will be socially beneficial is used to justify lobbying, deregulation and weakening of fundamental and individual rights protections for the sake of innovation. Here, happiness can also serve as a balancing factor within the strong risk mitigation approach taken in EU tech policy. The current approach predominantly takes a narrow focus on reducing risks rather than ensuring concrete, positive impacts from AI products and services. Happiness can create a ‘floor’ for policy-making to ensure AI is socially beneficial, not only less risky. The fact that a technology is less harmful does not mean it is socially beneficial.

When administering penalties, regulators and judges must take individual circumstances into consideration. For example, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) traditionally receive lower fines than multi-national companies. Illegal actions committed with malice or intent are punished more severely than those resulting from negligence. If technologies harm people's happiness measured in terms of relatedness, competence or autonomy, penalties should reflect this fact. Regulators and judges could, for example, require changes to the design of a product to mitigate specific harms to these three antecedents of happiness. AI data centre operators found to have misreported resource usage or environmental impact, for example, could face steeper fines owing to the downstream impact their actions have on residents' access to nature ( §5.1 ).

User empowerment, choice and literacy are important factors in people making decisions about how and to what extent they want to integrate technology into their lives. The three antecedents of happiness can help end users make these difficult decisions. Through public awareness campaigns and knowledge transfer, people can be encouraged to ask themselves questions like: will this technology enable me to make closer social or nature connections? Will it help me to master a new skill, and does it require dependency (e.g. generative AI)? Will it help me form and pursue life goals? Overall, will it make me happier?

The antecedents of happiness can help the AI industry. Relatedness, competence and autonomy can guide how products and services are designed and deployed, and serve as a counterweight to economic incentives and socially harmful business models. Companies should focus more on developing products that promote these three concepts, albeit without taking a simplistic or paternalistic approach (e.g. forcing users of a social networking app to contact friends once a day to improve relatedness). 77 Technologies are, of course, already designed with them in mind, but are often backed by harmful business models or features that outweigh their benefits to happiness. For example, dating and friendship apps enable human connection, digital libraries and online lectures enable learning and mastery of new skills, and health tracking apps enable people to achieve their health or life goals. Each of these examples coexists with socially harmful design choices meant to maximize profit or engagement at the cost of user well-being, such as ‘swiping’ behaviour on dating apps or excessive gamification of health goals.

People often struggle to understand and predict what makes them happy. Offloading cognitive work by using an LLM to write an essay for school may appear immediately beneficial to a stressed student. Connecting with a chatbot to alleviate loneliness might also seem like a good replacement for human connection. However, people require support to make sensible choices in such scenarios that will lead to more fulfilled lives.

Happiness research can provide such support if embedded in school curricula, AI literacy obligations, or similar learning opportunities. Some countries have already invested in this direction; Delhi, India, for example, implemented the Happiness Curriculum in 2018, which focuses on holistic learning aims rather than strictly academic outcomes [ 363 ]. 78 In Germany, a research project at TU Braunschweig advocates for integration of daily ‘happiness lessons’ into the curriculum [ 365 ]. While not a formal subject in school, the UK also urges investments in resources for well-being and mental health for students, and expects schools to cover mental health issues as part of the relationships and sex education and health education curriculum [ 366 ]. Based on our findings, we recommend further rollout of such initiatives with a specific focus on the role of emerging technologies in happiness and how to make sensible decisions about personal use.

These proposals are ambitious and open to future interpretation. Many key questions of implementation, measurement and enforcement are intentionally left open for future work. 79 While fully developing and justifying the necessary evidentiary, policy, organizational and technical requirements to implement and enforce these proposals in practice goes beyond the scope of this article, together they provide an initial direction for future research and policy-making efforts to rebalance EU tech policy in favour of social well-being.

Much like the legend of Perseus, the myth of self-made tech billionaires collapses under closer scrutiny. Whereas Perseus required divine gifts to slay Medusa, modern AI companies benefit from the substantial public subsidies lavished upon them by adoring governments. Perseus smartly honoured his divine patrons in thanks for their assistance, yet the same cannot be said of companies benefiting from the people underwriting the current AI boom. This technology may indeed lead to the unfettered economic growth and efficiency predicted by companies, but its impact on society, individual rights and well-being, employment, the environment and other public goods remains far more uncertain and looks increasingly harmful. The public seems to be left blindly subsidizing an international AI ‘arms race’ which will, at best, indirectly benefit them, and at worst actively harm them. Just like the heroes of ancient Greece, AI companies should fear losing ‘divine’ favour if their benefactors feel they have been taken for granted.

The public is in all but name a shareholder of AI companies. 80 To re-establish an appropriate balance between economic and social benefits in EU tech policy, we have proposed a new mandate and metric: happiness. Our proposal is an attempt to rebalance the focus of regulators from predominantly economic considerations towards a more holistic idea of societal progress. Being happy is a goal in itself, but happy people are also good for society. Happiness allows people to learn, work, create, care and participate well in families, schools, workplaces and communities. They are better learners, employees, problem-solvers, more helpful people and better able to build strong social relationships [ 328 , p. 825]. Happiness is a driver of many of the outcomes that governments, legislators and industry leaders already value.

Policymakers should increasingly prioritize relatedness, competence and autonomy as antecedents of happiness to ensure that public support goes to innovation that genuinely improves human happiness and well-being. These goals can be equally beneficial for companies and users themselves, helping guide better decisions which deliver economic and social benefits in tandem, rather than at the expense of one another. Making technology less harmful does not mean it is socially beneficial on balance. The AI industry must be compelled to aim higher, to actively enhance human well-being and fundamental and individual rights with innovation, rather than merely erode them less than originally projected.

Adam Smith, considered by many to be the ‘father’ of capitalism, already recognized this tension in the 18th century. He understood happiness as ‘tranquillity and enjoyment’, and argued that ‘disorders of human life…arise from over-rating the difference between one permanent situation and another’, meaning that the pursuit of improvements to a society's standard of living can undermine its residents’ happiness. See [ 168 , p. 149], [ 169 , p. 310], [ 170 , p. 71], [ 171–173 ].

Adam Smith, for example, observed that as soon as such key basic goods are guaranteed with sufficient wealth (including throughout old age), acquiring more wealth for its own sake should be avoided. Rather, he advises people to focus on the enjoyment of leisurely time and tranquillity [ 168 , 169 , p. 310], [ 170 , p. 9]. Other influential theorists acknowledge the tension between growth and happiness, and warn against the dangers of unfettered economic growth. John Stuart Mill, John Maynard Keynes and John Rawls agree that after a certain living standard is achieved, other pursuits should be prioritized over economic growth. Unfettered growth compromises happiness, leisurely time and justice. See [ 177 , pp. 478–479].

Joseph Stiglitz, for example, has observed that rapid economic growth in the USA in recent decades has predominantly benefited the rich, with the ‘average’ American financially worse off and earning less in real terms than 60 years ago. See [ 178 ]. Policies on education, minimum wage, more stringent tax systems, workers’ rights and anti-discrimination laws are necessary to prevent inequality and increase the welfare of the public. See [ 167 , p. 147]. Thomas Piketty has similarly examined how unfettered economic growth leads to wealth concentration; see [ 166 , p. 25]. More recently, these phenomena have been referred to as the ‘K-shaped’ US economy, with a privileged few responsible for an increasing proportion of spending despite the ‘average’ person being worse off in terms of disposable income. See [ 179 , 180 ].

Adam Smith advocated for a ‘sufficientarian’ standard rather than an egalitarian one, observing that ‘no society can surely be flourishing and happy, of which the far greater part of the members are poor and miserable’. See [ 185 , p. 78]. Modern economists have picked up and reinforced the importance of reducing inequality as an enabler of economic growth. See [ 169 , pp. 315–317], [ 186 , pp. 54–55], [ 187 , pp. 39–41].

Documents were identified through manual searching of company websites. We reviewed documents published or sponsored by IBM, Google, DeepMind, Microsoft, OpenAI, Amazon Web Services, Nvidia and Anthropic. For each document, we describe its vision for AI (i.e. near- and long-term predictions about the value of generative AI), strategies for implementation and usage (e.g. advice, best practices and insights about generative AI to fulfil aims and objectives) and beneficial use cases.

With regard to vision, most of the reviewed documents describe a vision of generative AI focused on the return on investment and gaining competitive advantages. Described motivations include increasing financial returns, ensuring AI leadership and finding new ways to scale or speed up processes and improve efficiency. None of the reviewed reports focuses on longer-term predictions or visions for AI, with the exception of one document published by Google Cloud [ 122 ].

With regard to strategies, most focus on adoption of AI by a business or organization for optimizing or automating processes, or upskilling where success rate can be measured empirically (e.g. claims regarding process efficiency and faster deployment of new technologies). Comparisons are drawn between ML and generative AI ‘innovations’ focused on improved task efficiency, such as data analysis or document processing. Little attention is given to the reliability or social, ethical or legal factors of AI systems in sales materials, which may instead be dealt with predominantly in research, technical reports and policy white papers. 81

With regard to use cases, the absence of descriptions of concrete, socially beneficial use cases in most of the reviewed promotional materials was notable. They lacked clear descriptions of mechanisms by which predicted social benefits will be delivered (i.e. more than ‘economic growth’, ‘competitiveness’ or ‘efficiency’ as being inherently good). One notable exception is a list maintained by Google Cloud which as of 22 April 2026 lists 1302 use cases of generative AI by organizations worldwide; however, even here concrete details of social benefits are lacking, with each use case receiving a one- to two-sentence description. 82 The focus was instead on high-level descriptions of types of tasks or work that might support specific outcomes (e.g. automated document summarization to increases employee productivity). Across these higher-level descriptions, AI was said to improve customer satisfaction and interactions, employee productivity and efficiency of work processes.

Although unfamiliar to many, ‘happiness’ and related concepts like ‘well-being’ already serve as guiding principles for public policy decision-making in many countries, balanced with economic growth or GDP. None of these examples can be categorically endorsed as the ‘correct’ approach to mandating happiness as a public policy goal owing to vagueness, controversies, implementation challenges, methodological criticisms and other flaws; for example, some approaches reductively equate happiness and well-being with economic growth. Nonetheless, their existence shows that the concept has some traction within policy-making internationally as a foil to a myopic focus on economic growth and GDP.

Policy mandates to measure and improve well-being or happiness have been adopted in several countries. Perhaps the best-known case of a public policy happiness mandate comes from Bhutan. Happiness is explicitly measured through the Gross National Happiness (GNH) index, defined by nine happiness measures (or ‘bowls’) [ 367 ], 83 which are further operationalized via 33 indicators [ 367 ]. 84 An individual is considered happy if they possess at least 66% in all the 33 weighted indicators and ‘bowls’ [ 369 , p. 1]. 85 Bhutan conducts surveys every 3–5 years to assess these measures and indicators. Survey results help guide public policy decisions, the allocation of resources and aim to incentivize NGOs and businesses to focus more on happiness and well-being rather than purely economic growth [ 367 ].

Following Bhutan's shift from an absolute monarchy to a democratic constitutional monarchy, many policies and laws informed by these happiness measures have been introduced from 2008 onwards [ 368 , pp. 492–493, 504]. For example, GNH measures are clearly reflected in Bhutan's current 5-year public policy plan, which prioritizes climate resilience, vocational training, education, healthcare, digital transformation, resilience and governance [ 370 , pp. 4–7]. Their national AI strategy similarly shows influence from the GNH, focusing on ‘holistic wellbeing, sustainability and cultural preservation’ among other goals [ 371 , p. 7]. This holistic approach (‘GNH centric design’) prioritizes AI in key areas like agriculture, tourism and energy, health, education and public services, natural resources and biodiversity, culture and language [ 371 , p. 8].

Other countries have adopted similar mandates, but under the heading of ‘well-being’. A 2009 report by the Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Commission on ‘the limits of GDP as an indicator of economic performance and social progress’ influenced several countries’ approaches to measuring and mandating improvements to well-being. The report advocates for the inclusion of universal ‘quality of life’ measures when assessing social progress [ 372 ]. 86

In 2017, Italy became the first OECD country to explicitly include considerations of well-being and happiness alongside economic considerations when taking public policy and budgetary decisions [ 374 , p. 3]. Italy adapted the report's recommended universal measures into 12 indicators of well-being ( table 2 ), 87 which can be revised over time [ 374 , p. 12].

In 2021, Ireland similarly developed a ‘Well-being Framework’ inspired by the Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Commission, with 11 indicators measured ( table 2 ) every 4–5 years [ 373 ], [ 376 , p. 3], [ 377 ]. 88 Policymakers are directed to factor results into their decisions. Example affected policy measures include a carbon tax, 89 revisions to the tax and welfare system and equality measures (e.g. around gender and age) [ 376 , p. V].

Other approaches draw a simpler direct connection between well-being and economic considerations. For example, in 2019, New Zealand introduced a ‘Wellbeing Budget’ focusing on domestic challenges including mental health, domestic violence and child poverty, support for Māori and Pacific people (e.g. skills and income), digital transformation and productivity, and low-emissions business transformation [ 378 , p. 6]. In 2025, the Public Finance Act 1989 was then amended to require ‘social, economic, environmental and cultural’ well-being considerations to be included in budgetary decision-making [ 379 , para. 26 M]. The improvement of living standards (e.g. health, education, good working conditions, cultural protection, leisure time, friends and family, housing, environmental protection, firms and markets, and good governance) is also linked to ‘well-being’ and ought to guide policy and budgetary decisions [ 380 ]. Nepal has also mandated improved well-being in economic terms via its ‘Prosperous Nepal, Happy Nepali’ plan, which aims to make Nepal a high-income country by 2043. Nepal does not granularly measure happiness, but instead defines it broadly as the realization of higher living standards (e.g. higher income, better healthcare and education, physical infrastructure) and socialist values [ 381 , pp. 4–5, 25].

It is worth remembering that, as discussed above ( §5.3 ), economic considerations are relevant antecedents of happiness, for example, in relation to fulfilment of basic needs, but only to the point of diminishing returns. Further, they are not as strong predictors as other concepts like relatedness, competence and autonomy.

In some countries, well-being and happiness are measured solely for informational and guidance purposes, rather than as part of a public policy mandate. OECD member states, for example, participate in the ‘OECD Well-being Framework’, which compares well-being between countries over time based on measurements across 11 dimensions ( table 2 ) [ 382 , 383 ]. OECD countries do sometimes integrate well-being measurements into policy and budgetary processes, but not owing to a legal mandate [ 374 , p. 14], [ 376 , p. 3].

Similarly, the United Kingdom Office for National Statistics started collecting ‘well-being’ data in 2010 across 10 dimensions and 60 indicators ( table 2 ). 90 The well-being data are intended to inform policymakers and help make decisions, understand the impact of certain actions (e.g. building a new airport) [ 386 ], and otherwise guide the Treasury [ 384 ]. However, unlike Italy and Ireland, policymakers are not legally mandated to use the data to improve societal well-being; rather, it serves as guidance or a checklist to assess competing economic and well-being interests in a fair manner (e.g. the value of a measure and its cost) [ 387 ].

This section does not claim to offer a comprehensive picture or assessment of the efficacy of these public policy ‘happiness’ and ‘well-being’ strategies. 91 However, we have shown that happiness as a public policy compass is not a completely foreign concept. We have surveyed a range of approaches to measure and improve the well-being of the public, ranging from policies that are inspired by religious values and connection with nature to relationships with people and opportunities for choiceful living. These must, of course, be evaluated alongside the concrete social problems facing regions, economic well-being indicators and the improvement of living standards and quality of life. The concepts of relatedness, competence and autonomy are self-evidently reflected, if not explicitly mentioned, in many of these general social policies. 92

The tale of Perseus and Medusa is a classic of Greek mythology. Perseus, son of divine parentage, is a strong and fearless hero who journeys to slay Medusa, a feared monster whose mere gaze can turn living beings into stone.

Yet on closer inspection, the tale of a seemingly self-made hero ridding the world of evil is much more complicated [ 1 ]. Perseus did not work alone—he had the benefit of divine intervention throughout his journey. He received a cap of invisibility from Hades, winged shoes from Hermes, a sword from Hephaestus and a shield, enchanted bag and strategic counsel from Athena. Perseus could not have slain Medusa by himself, and yet he is traditionally hailed as a self-made hero, an aspirational symbol of Greek heroism [ 1 ].

Today, similar myths are crafted about the founders and chief executive officers of major technology companies. These self-invented quasi-gods are said to make the impossible possible. They wield the power to shape society through their products and innovation, anticipating and solving problems the public cannot yet see.

However, just like Perseus, these ‘self-made’ billionaires rely on substantial outside help. Beyond their investors, mentors, employees and others, tech leaders rely on substantial ‘divine’ assistance from the state and public. More often than not, this help is given without consulting the public who ultimately pays for it. Whereas Perseus would not dream of ignoring his divine patrons, tech leaders readily pretend their public benefactors do not exist, perhaps to protect the myth of the ‘self-made’ genius.

Our focus is on AI-relevant tech policy and the AI industry in the EU. 1 As a region known (rightly or wrongly) for having very stringent technology regulation, it would be reasonable to expect it to have the most favourable balance between industrial and societal interests.

The public is in all but name a shareholder of AI companies. We first map some of the subsidies handed out on behalf of the public to make companies successful in the EU, including tax breaks, governmental funding, tariffs on foreign goods, access to public infrastructure, selling or lending land to build data centres and deregulation of labour, data protection, environmental and intellectual property (IP) laws. In particular, the recently proposed Digital Omnibus grants the AI industry substantial regulatory relief justified by vague promises of economic growth and increased competitiveness. Next, we review the predicted benefits of AI according to AI companies: economic growth, support for innovation 2 and increased productivity and competitiveness of businesses and markets. In contrast, we find that the predicted social benefits are highly uncertain, resist precise measurement (and therefore future enforcement or redress) and are of dubious value.

We then review current tech policy to understand how predicted benefits and risks are balanced to protect EU values and rights (i.e. societal interests) while still enabling innovation (i.e. industrial interests). We find that EU tech policy generally takes a risk mitigation approach, which aims to measure and minimize the risks of new technologies, and thereby strike a balance between individual and social interests on the one hand, and industrial interests on the other. Policymakers assume that innovation will be socially beneficial and therefore justify its risks, but fail to ensure this balance in practice or demand concrete benefits from the AI industry. This is problematic as EU policymakers have a mandate to act in the best interests of the public, but are currently doing so under extreme uncertainty. 3

We argue that this strong risk mitigation approach is ill-suited to address the predicted risks of AI in a holistic manner. The key problem is that less risky technologies are not necessarily socially beneficial, so continuing mainly with this current risk mitigation and balancing approach will not guarantee AI will be socially beneficial. This outcome is unacceptable given the actual, substantial costs already imposed on the public via subsidies in the name of innovation.

Current policy targets specific, concrete, measurable risks and how best to manage and mitigate them, but struggles to counteract less tangible, well-defined or acute risks. Many of the benefits and risks posed by AI are vague, open-ended, cumulative, longitudinal and difficult to measure. To continue serving its intended function, EU tech policy must adapt to address them. This is not to say that the current risk-based approach needs to be abandoned, but rather that it must be complemented with aspirational and positive goals that work to counteract the vaguely defined, open-ended risks posed by general-purpose AI.

Current policy is defined by two goals: (i) fundamental and individual rights and EU values, and (ii) innovation and free market competition. Risks posed to the first by the second must be balanced through rules and restrictions on technology development, deployment and governance. The weakness of this approach is that risks must be well-defined and measurable to be mitigated through regulatory measures. We advocate for a third, aspirational goal to be added: happiness. This additional goal will serve as a precautionary safeguard to balance against the highly uncertain and under-researched cumulative effects of AI on society. We focus on happiness as a subcategory of individual well-being. Happiness is an ideal policy goal that already features internationally in public policy-making ( appendix B ), which reflects individual well-being and contributes to social well-being, as we discuss below. 4

To unpack how and why this is a goal worth pursuing, we first examine a prominent meta-theory of human motivation and well-being within psychology—self-determination theory (SDT)—which has shown large global effects predicting happiness and other forms of well-being across 50 years of empirical research in psychology. ‘Relatedness’, ‘competence’ and ‘autonomy’ are three antecedents of happiness that have been described across diverse psychological theories in recent decades. They are viewed as innate psychological needs that serve as preconditions for people's happiness [ 2 , 3 ]. SDT provides a parsimonious explanatory framework to define how the environment supports or thwarts happiness, which extends to different domains of life (e.g. work and relationships) and levels of analysis (e.g. interpersonal, institutional and structural). These concepts can help determine whether AI can actually make people happier both in theory and practice, and thus whether it is actually worth the significant public and private investment seen in recent years from the perspective of individual happiness and social well-being.

We conclude by exploring how these psychological theories of happiness can be woven into policy considerations. We argue that happiness should be introduced as an additional public good that should be prioritized by legislators when regulating AI alongside traditional risk mitigation and economic considerations. Promoting and protecting the happiness of the public should be an overarching principle guiding the allocation of public resources (e.g. land, tax breaks, data, infrastructure and funding) as well as the drafting and enforcement of laws. Happiness should also guide efforts in AI literacy meant to enhance user autonomy, incentivize design choices when developing new products and feature on syllabi in schools.

The AI industry enjoys a growing range of subsidies to improve its competitiveness and support deployment of AI products and services across the EU single market. We use the term ‘subsidy’ broadly to refer to actions and incentives by policymakers that benefit the AI industry while simultaneously weakening fundamental or individual rights protections or otherwise imposing tangible or opportunity costs on the public. Some of these actions are ‘direct’ subsidies involving governments giving money to companies, whereas others are ‘indirect’ subsidies or aid which bring financial or non-monetary benefits for companies. Subsidies take the form of economic, political and regulatory incentives granted on behalf of the general public. This advantageous environment has been constructed through a combination of lobbying, policy-making and (lack of) legal enforcement.

AI companies are subsidized by a range of mechanisms, including privileged access to public goods and resources such as access to governmental or public data [ 4 ] and buying or lending land to build data centres [ 5 ]; (free) access to public infrastructure, favourable research conditions and public investment in infrastructure (e.g. gigafactories), research and startups; favourable research conditions; various tax incentives [ 6 , pp. 53–54], [ 7–11 ]; 5 tariffs on foreign goods; 6 relaxation and deregulation of legal standards and duties in tech and human right laws [ 14 ], environmental law [ 15 , 16 ], 7 copyright protection [ 18 ], labour law [ 19 ], [ 20 , pp. 3–4] and merger and competition law [ 21 ], [ 22 , pp. 6–9], [ 23–25 ]; and unregulated political capture [ 26 , 27 ]. All of these advantages enable their success in the market, and the public either directly or indirectly pays for them. In other words, these are the costs paid by the public to enable technological innovation.

Throughout this section, we focus on subsidies offered by the EU. We do, however, include some examples from other regions as they reveal the types of subsidies being granted to AI companies, as well as the way such subsidies can impact the public in the future. 8

To further enable expansion of cloud computing and AI capacity, the EU has introduced plans to support the construction of data centres across Europe through various incentives and weakened regulatory requirements. Data centres create capacity for both private and public (e.g. scientific and governmental) computing and storage needs, and serve as essential infrastructure for many key Internet and computing services and platforms. However, where these incentives are intended to expand computing capacity specifically for generative AI products and services, questions must be asked about whether the technology's proposed benefits justify the costs imposed on the public ( §3 ).

The EU's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CAIDA) aims to triple European data centre capacity over the next 5–7 years. CAIDA will fast-track building permits and ease access to energy infrastructure and financial aid for companies. The Act follows a December 2025 proposal to streamline the permitting process and exempt many tech infrastructure projects from environmental assessments entirely to meet ‘pressing geopolitical and competitiveness challenges’ [ 14 , p. 1]. 9 These and related plans to weaken or not enforce existing environmental legal standards are predicted to cost the general public between €180 billion and €325 billion per year through forgone benefits, while saving affected companies €1 billion per year. 10

Proposals to weaken environmental and permitting standards have faced significant criticism in recognition of their costs for the general public [ 5 ]. These types of incentives threaten to raise prices and limit general public access to scarce resources. 11 Across Europe, residents already compete with data centre developers for water, land and electricity resources, for example, in Spain, Germany, the UK, Italy, The Netherlands, France as well as Ireland, where data centres already account for 22% of national annual electricity consumption and consume more than all urban households combined [ 5 , 32 ]. The general public is already losing access to (semi-)natural land (e.g. forests and agricultural land) and facing increased electricity and water demand from data centres that outstrips available supply [ 33 ]. In the USA, residents are losing access to clean water [ 34 ].

In many cases, governments justify these increased costs and competition with the employment opportunities and economic benefits data centres are predicted to bring to local and regional communities. Unfortunately, benefits often fail to materialize. In Romania and North Holland, jobs promised by data centre companies, which received financial and environmental incentives from local authorities, were extremely limited. 12 In the USA, companies have received various tax exemptions worth tens of millions of dollars in the past to build data centres. These exemptions caused budgetary gaps for local governments and yet created only a handful of jobs in return, 13 with some states currently reconsidering them [ 40 ].

New EU laws like the recast Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) will do little to correct the imbalanced incentives currently enjoyed by the AI industry. The EED creates environmental reporting duties but does not secure adequate public access, meaning companies can keep their sustainability figures secret [ 41–43 ]. It likewise fails to impose binding EU-wide efficiency targets for data centres, relying instead on Member States to set local targets and initial enforcement may be lax. 14 The reporting metrics used are also deeply flawed and fail to capture the actual energy consumption and relative efficiency of data centres [ 46 ].

AI companies also benefit from widespread access to public datasets. Frontier and generative AI models in particular are trained on data scraped from the open Internet as well as public and private repositories of books, articles, academic papers and other written materials. Companies currently benefit from relaxed enforcement and interpretation of relevant copyright and IP laws [ 47–49 ], although court cases remain pending, concerning the rights of companies and copyright holders [ 50 ].

Access to public and government datasets is often provided through contracts to provide essential public IT services or infrastructure. DeepMind and Palantir, for example, have won controversial access to public health data in the UK to build platforms for the National Health Service [ 4 , 51 , 52 ]. In the EU, Google, Microsoft and Amazon Web Services are the main providers for cloud computing services for governments. Critics have warned that the current US administration will compel companies to transfer EU data to the USA, with such requests already rapidly increasing [ 53 , 54 ]. 15 Some Member States are already calling for divestment in the name of digital sovereignty [ 55 ]. 16 The public is rarely directly consulted or able to challenge such contracts even though it is their data being accessed and their rights being impacted.

The EU is actively working to increase public spending on AI and data centres to improve competition and reduce reliance on US and Chinese companies. In 2025, the EU launched the InvestAI initiative to mobilize €200 billion of investment in AI infrastructure (e.g. gigafactories), research and startups, €50 billion of which comes directly from taxes [ 8 , 59 , 60 ]. A further €1 billion is being repurposed from existing financing programmes in support of the ‘Apply AI Strategy’, which aims to improve European productivity, competitiveness and technological sovereignty. 17 This follows a 2025 policy proposal to enable the redirection of existing ‘unused’ tax funds to invest into ‘AI Gigafactory projects and facilities, and for the creation of multi-site gigafactories across multiple countries’ [ 62 , 63 ]. These decisions impose significant opportunity costs, as these are public funds that could be used elsewhere to create immediate, tangible benefits for the public.

Beyond direct financing, AI companies also benefit from significant tax breaks and exemptions, which lessen their tax burden and thus their contribution to the state and public goods. Profits from digital activities are often not taxed owing to many companies not having a physical presence in the EU [ 64 ]. AI companies nonetheless generate substantial revenue from the data of EU citizens and residents.

The need for a new tax system to close this gap has been previously recognized by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which proposed a global minimum rate of effective corporate tax of 15% in 2021. 18 This proposal was subsequently adopted by the EU and put into force in 2024 [ 65 ]. Many EU countries have also recently introduced separate digital services taxes. 19 These taxes average between 3 and 5% and cover activities such as online advertising, data sales, digital intermediation services that facilitate the exchange of goods or services and on-demand audio-visual media services. 20

While these appear to be promising steps taken by the EU to ensure multi-national AI companies pay their fair share towards public goods, the USA has successfully lobbied against them. As of 2026, US-based multi-national tech companies have been exempted from the OECD's 15% global corporate tax [ 66 , 67 ]. In July 2025, the EU abandoned plans to introduce an EU-wide digital tax, potentially owing to pressure from the Trump administration in trade deal negotiations happening in parallel [ 11 ]. US multi-national tech companies thus continue to enjoy a lower tax burden while expanding data centres and AI offerings across Europe.

Regulatory frameworks are only as effective as the political willingness to enforce them. Tech companies have long complained that compliance with relevant frameworks can be complex, resource-intensive and prone to uncertainty owing to the vagueness of legal requirements. With newly introduced frameworks such as the Digital Services Act (DSA) and Digital Markets Act (DMA), many multi-national tech companies are going a step further in refusing or delaying compliance with many requirements. These companies are, thus far, only facing fines and investigations by the European Commission while still being allowed to operate in the EU single market despite planned or declared non-compliance. 21 This leniency in enforcement can be considered yet another type of advantage enjoyed by major tech companies.

The DSA aims to reduce the social and systemic harms of online platforms and search engines, including misinformation, disinformation, negative impacts on political processes, child safety, gender-based violence, illegal content and human rights violations [ 69–72 ]. Early reports suggest many multi-national tech companies are refusing to fully comply with the DSA, with both the compliance picture and active investigations by the EU Commission changing rapidly [ 73–75 ].

With regard to disinformation and fact-checking obligations under the DSA's Code of Practice, for example, Microsoft and Google are reported to have refused to meet fact-checking obligations [ 73 , 76 , 77 ]. TikTok and Meta are currently under investigation by the European Commission [ 78 , 79 ], with the latter having ceased third-party fact-checking on Facebook, Instagram and Threads in the USA in early 2025 [ 80 ]. According to reporting from early 2025, Google, Microsoft and TikTok ‘have withdrawn from all commitments related to political advertising, citing their current ban on political ads’, and are likewise refusing to meet requirements to ‘develop, fund and collaborate with an independent third-party body to enable data access for researchers’ [ 73 ]. A September 2025 report from the European Fact-Checking Standards Network found that many platforms are either ignoring or formally abandoning fact-checking commitments but still presenting as signatories to the DSA Code of Practice [ 81 ]. 22

AI companies also enjoy leniency with regard to the DMA, which is intended to revive healthy market competition and reduce monopolistic behaviour. Many companies are considered ‘gatekeepers’ under the DMA, meaning they face a range of platform and service governance obligations. Initial analysis of compliance reports submitted by major tech companies, including Amazon, Microsoft and Meta, in 2026 found that they have thus far failed to make major changes to their compliance strategies as gatekeepers, and instead are taking a cautious and slow approach to compliance [ 82 ].

These are only a few recent examples of seemingly anti-competitive behaviour that went unpunished. AI companies routinely buy up their rivals before they become a threat (e.g. Meta buying WhatsApp and Instagram, and Google buying DoubleClick) [ 83 ]. While this behaviour is understandable from a business point of view, it is worrying from a consumer protection standpoint. Monopolies are a danger to ‘market competitiveness’ and ‘consumer welfare’ [ 84 ]. Competition authorities are tasked with investigating and preventing such mergers that would harm the market and consumers. Any failure to strongly enforce competition law can therefore be treated as a passive advantage enjoyed by tech companies at the cost of consumer welfare.

In Europe and the USA, authorities have generally treated potential tech mergers permissively in recent years. Examples include the EU Commission's approval of Google's acquisition of Photomath in 2023 [ 85 ] and Wiz in 2026 [ 21 ], Microsoft's acquisition of Activision Blizzard in 2023 [ 86 ] and Amazon's acquisition of MGM in 2022 [ 87 ]. While there are still cases where the Commission has prevented mergers such as the acquisition of iRobot by Amazon [ 88 ], many mergers proceed uninhibited [ 83 , 84 , 89 ]. The Microsoft–Mistral partnership also successfully avoided a merger investigation by the UK authorities in 2023 [ 90 ].

Emerging AI monopolies also appear to be receiving leniency in the USA. The AI industry is deeply circularly invested, with hundreds of billions of dollars being exchanged between 10 major AI companies [ 91 , 92 ]. For example, by 2023, both Amazon ($4 billion) and Google ($2 billion) invested heavily in Anthropic, a relatively new AI start-up [ 93 ]. As part of an anti-trust case against Google for potential monopolization of the search industry, in 2025 the US Department of Justice proposed that Google should be required to divest from AI competitors including Anthropic, but subsequently walked back the proposal [ 93 ]. 23 In 2026, Google announced a further $40 billion investment into Anthropic [ 95 ].

Recent years have seen a strong push to weaken existing and proposed EU technology-relevant laws. The push for deregulation has come both internally from EU Member States such as Germany [ 96 ], France [ 97 ], Sweden [ 98 ] and Denmark [ 99 ], but also externally from the USA and multi-national technology companies [ 100 ]. Lobbying efforts have focused on revising and weakening the EU AI Act, DSA [ 101 ], privacy laws including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and proposed ePrivacy Regulation [ 102 ], 24 non-discrimination law, liability frameworks [ 104 , 105 ] and environmental sustainability standards relevant to data centre construction [ 33 ].

A key result of these efforts is the newly proposed and heavily lobbied Digital Omnibus, which will replace or amend some of these and other laws with the stated goal of simplifying the legal landscape for technology companies to increase competitiveness, streamline legal compliance, support the growth of micro-, small- and medium-sized enterprises and thus unleash the ‘full potential’ of AI [ 106 ]. 25 If adopted, the Omnibus will create a much friendlier data protection environment for companies. 26 It will establish (i) data protection privileges and exceptions for (commercial) research 27 and the training of (general-purpose) AI models, 28 (ii) relaxed data protection standards for pseudonymized data and biometric processing (i.e. special category data), 29 (iii) tighter restrictions on access rights for data subjects, 30 (iv) limitations on the definitional scope of personal data, 31 and (v) weakened protections against automated decision-making. 32

Other areas of EU law have also been weakened. A group of EU Member States blocked an amendment to non-discrimination law which would have strengthened protections against (AI-driven) discrimination based on religion, belief, disability, age and sexual orientation [ 110 ]. 33 The proposed AI Liability Directive, which would have complemented the existing Product Liability Directive with rules tailored to AI systems, suffered a similar fate [ 111 ], as did the ePrivacy Regulation, which was withdrawn following lobbying by advertising, telecoms and technology companies, as well as some EU Member States [ 103 ].

These trends are, of course, nothing new. Lobbying has strongly impacted the regulation of Internet platforms; a recent study by Falkner shows that, since 2022, the EU has consistently sided with the interests of the AI industry (i.e. platform providers) over the public [ 101 ]. A 2026 study by Birhane et al. [ 27 ] provides further evidence of political capture by the tech industry. While proponents of deregulation have hailed these trends as essential cutting of ‘red tape’ to facilitate innovation, 34 human rights advocates have argued that they equally weaken individual rights by creating loopholes and gaps for industry to exploit [ 113 ]. 35

The ‘revolving door’ between industry and policy-making in recent decades has enabled the political capture essential to construct and maintain the subsidized environment for the tech industry discussed throughout this section. Recent notable examples in the EU include Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Aura Salla, the former Director of EU Policy at Meta from 2020 to 2023, who joined the European Parliament in 2024 and has been acting as rapporteur on the controversial Digital Omnibus proposal since 2026. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) are calling for her removal from this position [ 26 , 115 ]. Further, Niamh Sweeney, who has held positions in tech companies such as Meta (2015–2021) and Stripe (2021–2022), was appointed in 2025 as Irish Data Protection Commissioner [ 116 ]. The UK also has many high-profile examples. 36

The AI industry benefits from many subsidies to enable innovation and deployment of AI products and services. At the same time, they argue that failing to deregulate will continue to stifle innovation and place the EU at a competitive disadvantage globally in the AI ‘arms race’. The common narrative that the ‘EU regulates while the world innovates’ is being deployed to support deregulation, premised on the unreliable claim that innovation and regulation cannot coexist [ 118–120 ]. The public thus faces high costs for enabling AI, but what is it promised in return?

To begin to understand the vision of AI currently being sold to (i) businesses, (ii) the public sector, and (iii) the general public, we reviewed a non-comprehensive sample of recent promotional materials (e.g. reports, sales materials, press releases, product briefings and other grey literature) published or sponsored by major AI companies including IBM, Google, DeepMind, Microsoft, OpenAI, Amazon Web Services, Nvidia and Anthropic (see appendix A for an overview of reviewed documents). Given their recency, these documents predominantly focus on general-purpose or generative AI. We find that the main selling points for AI across these companies and sectors are economic, while little attention is given to justifying the social and regulatory costs of the technology, and concrete details of socially beneficial use cases and their underlying mechanisms remain rare.

The reviewed documents focused heavily on AI products and services for businesses. AI companies espouse broad visions for the future of AI driving substantial economic growth [ 121 , p. 10], [ 122 , pp. 4–5], enhanced productivity and competition [ 122 , pp. 4–5], [ 123 , p. 4], [ 124 , p. 2], greater speed and efficiency by automating existing processes or work 37 and improved data-driven insights and decision-making [ 121 , p. 4]. Predicting the future economic impact of AI is of course difficult, but a 2023 study sponsored by Microsoft claimed that ‘[f]or every $1 companies invest in AI, they are realizing an average of $3.5 in return, and 5% of organizations worldwide are realizing an average of an average $8 in return’ [ 125 , p. 2]. Similarly, OpenAI has claimed that ‘AI leaders have seen 1.5x faster revenue growth, 1.6x higher shareholder returns, and 1.4x better return on invested capital than their less advanced peers’ [ 126 , p. 3].

Concrete and detailed use cases to substantiate these economic claims are rare in the reviewed documents. They instead focus on broad types of work (e.g. summarization, writing, data analysis, coding, visualizations and content creation) or business processes (e.g. personalized customer interactions, business operations, quality assurance and auditing) that can be improved [ 121 , p. 4], [ 123 , p. 4], [ 124 , pp. 2, 6], [ 126 , pp. 6–8, 11–24], [ 127 , p. 1]. Benefits are predicted across sectors including medicine, telecommunications, retail, manufacturing, finance, product design and software development [ 122 , p. 35], [ 127 , p. 1], [ 128 , p. 5].

AI companies are also interested in working with the public sector [ 129 , p. 37]. Many already have significant partnerships with government departments to provide products, public services and research. 38 Predictions made here echo those made for businesses, focusing on increasing productivity and efficiency of public bodies, 39 reducing unemployment [ 132 ], streamlined and automated workflows [ 129 , p. 37], [ 131 ], improved data-driven insights and analytics [ 129 , p. 37] and improvements to infrastructure and citizen services. 40 Work types to be automated include summarization [ 137 , p. 11], question-answering and fact-finding (e.g. public-facing first response chatbots) [ 134 ], [ 137 , p. 11], research [ 138 , p. 4], [ 139 ], writing [ 138 , p. 4] and mail sorting [ 134 ]. Again, detailed use cases are rare, with some companies highlighting high-level positive use cases in sectors such as health, science, education and government services [ 139 , p. 3], [ 140 ].

The general public is less of a focal point in the reviewed documents. Again, companies make vague predictions about high-level benefits such as economic growth, employment opportunities, upskilling and work optimization [ 126 , p. 3], [ 141 ]. The public is predicted to indirectly benefit from more efficient business and public processes, such as quicker answers to questions or access to information about government services [ 135 , 136 ]. 41 One of the most common predictions made by companies is that AI will improve customer satisfaction. 42

It is worth remembering that the aforementioned predictions about the impact of AI on medicine, research, education, content creation and similar areas will have downstream impacts on the public, both positive and negative. Individuals may be empowered to do their jobs more quickly or efficiently but may also face greater cognitive fatigue or competition for employment [ 143 , 144 ]. Whether these effects are ultimately beneficial to the public remains to be seen. 43

Across the reviewed documents, it is notable that the main selling points for (generative) AI are purely economic: economic growth, easier innovation and increased productivity and competitiveness. Companies offer limited discussion of non-economic benefits or the ‘public value’ offered by their technologies [ 145 , p. 114]. 44 Socially beneficial use cases are rarely discussed, and typically at a high level with little detail or evidence of positive impacts for the general public. 45 This gap is striking given the strong push to deregulate as well as the significant subsidies being given to the AI industry in the EU, all for the sake of enabling innovation. These choices come at the cost of public funds and fundamental rights, which is not reflected in the sales pitch of AI companies. Drawing inspiration from Prainsack's observation that the ‘public value’ of technologies is frequently left vague and contested [ 145 , p. 114], 46 we argue that public subsidies for AI require clear justification in these terms. Currently, it is not clear how the public will benefit from AI.

The AI industry is clearly promising substantial economic growth. What remains unclear is how these predictions will fare in the future. Empirical evidence of the economic impact of AI remains nascent. It is nonetheless useful to review early signals to understand possible pathways forward for the technology.

Many analysts have already cast doubt on the scale of AI's potential economic contribution. A 2024 report by Goldman Sachs noted that returns on investment are thus far slow, and efficiency gains from AI do not outweigh the costs of training and deploying increasingly large models, which would need to solve much more complex tasks to be profitable [ 148 ]. A subsequent 2025 report speculated that AI may already be fuelling a financial bubble [ 149 ]. The gross domestic product (GDP) boost over the next 10 years in the USA is predicted to be modest [ 150 ]. Deloitte published a report in the same year stating that executives across the EU and Middle East do not believe that generative AI will deliver a satisfactory return on investment in the next 2–4 years [ 151 ]. Similarly, a 2025 report from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) noted that ‘[d]espite $30–40 billion in enterprise investment into GenAI…95% of organizations are getting zero return’ and only ‘5% of integrated AI pilots are extracting millions in value’ [ 152 , p. 3]. With regard to productivity, a possible predictor of future growth, a 2026 survey of 6000+ C-suite executives across the USA, UK, Germany and Australia revealed that 90% reported that AI had no impact on productivity or employment at their daily business [ 153 ]. 47 In contrast, some experiments have shown increases in productivity and satisfaction in writing and customer support tasks [ 155 , 156 ].

While all of the above is preliminary evidence, it is important to remember that industrial and societal economic growth are not the same. Many providers of AI products and services, and underlying hardware and infrastructure, are currently experiencing rapid increases in value and market share, which would suggest the technology is contributing to economic growth [ 157 ]. However, individual AI companies growing does not guarantee sustained economic growth across society. Economic growth is not the same as economic equality. In this respect, concerns must already be raised that AI's disruptive effects could widen economic inequalities [ 150 ]. 48

Companies are also taking steps to reduce their liability for (non-)financial harms caused by their AI products and services, which would appear to undermine their claims about the inevitability of financial and productivity benefits. Microsoft, for example, initially stated in their Terms of Service that Copilot should be used only for ‘entertainment purposes’, despite being heavily marketed at the time as a tool that should increase productivity. 49 The terms and conditions further indemnify Microsoft against liability for inaccuracies or financial losses incurred from using Copilot. OpenAI, Google and Anthropic have added similar statements to their Terms of Service to shield themselves from potential liability. 50

Of course, any analysis of general-purpose and generative AI's potential economic impact must necessarily be treated as incomplete and preliminary at this stage. With that said, preliminary analysis appears to cast doubt on these technologies delivering substantial economic growth in the near term. This uncertainty is troubling because, while economic growth (and equality) is not guaranteed, the social and financial costs paid by the public to subsidize the AI industry are already very real and significant.

Regardless of its likelihood, the potential economic growth brought about by AI remains a key selling point, enabling innovation, increased productivity and competitiveness and other social goods. These ends seem inherently valuable for society at first glance. 51 However, the relationship between economic growth and social well-being is not simple. While growth can clearly contribute to public goods, for example, through greater taxation to fund improved public services (e.g. transportation and healthcare) or improved job opportunities for citizens, 52 economists have also long studied the relationship and frequent tension between growth and well-being, for example, through the lens of ‘welfare economics’. 53

Unlimited economic growth (through AI) is not necessarily desirable. Growth has instrumental value, measured by its contribution to goods such as liberty, security, basic needs (e.g. access to food, shelter, clothing) or time with friends, family and community [ 170 , pp. 10–11], [ 173 , pp. 832–833, 835]. Fulfilment of basic needs is a stronger predictor of well-being than income [ 174 ], while the contribution of wealth to happiness beyond certain thresholds varies by circumstance [ 175 , 176 ]. In other words, there may be such a thing as ‘enough’. 54

Simultaneously, unfettered pursuit of growth in recent decades has led to worsening economic and social inequality across countries. 55 This strongly indicates that economic growth from AI will not suddenly be equally shared across the people subsidizing it. Instead, it is likely that this pursuit will exacerbate both social and economic inequalities. 56 For many economists and social theorists, many forms of inequality are inherently bad and should be eradicated through social policies and governmental action (for our proposal, see §7 ). 57

The impact of economic growth brought about by AI on societal well-being is therefore an open question for the future despite confident but simplistic predictions from the AI industry. Economic growth can improve societal well-being if directed at the right societal goals by its creators, regulators and users. 58 EU policymakers have a significant role to play here. Proactive decision-making can ensure the benefits of AI are more equally shared across society. The reactive approach currently taken towards AI policy-making unfortunately leaves much to be desired in this regard.

A current popular narrative, often advanced by industry and policymakers, claims that regulation stifles innovation, whereas deregulation, lax regulatory enforcement and subsidies enable it. Setting aside the fact that this narrative is contested [ 118 , 188 ], it is concerning that individuals and society bear the main costs and risks of ‘enabling innovation’ in these terms without any guaranteed benefits [ 189 ]. As a result, people are more exposed to the risks of AI and less able to seek legal recourse when harmed than would otherwise be the case. The willingness of governments and policymakers to grant subsidies on behalf of the public while being aware of these risks would suggest that they see technological innovation as inherently or instrumentally beneficial to society and worth the costs imposed. These beliefs are evident in the trade-offs between rights and innovation struck across EU tech policy, balancing enablers of innovation with protections for the vital interests of society and individual rights.

To map these trade-offs and assess the extent to which policymakers view innovation as inherently or instrumentally valuable, we review recent EU tech policy relevant to AI ( table 1 ). These frameworks reveal how policymakers envision the role, value and risks of emerging technologies in society, including the risks of ‘hindering’ innovation through overly stringent regulation and failing to sufficiently invest public funds. 59 The general strategy pursued across the reviewed frameworks is risk mitigation. 60

The reviewed frameworks predict two types of benefits: (i) general economic growth, competitive advantages and digital sovereignty, or (ii) sector-specific economic and productivity benefits. Concerning the former, examples include the GDPR enabling the free flow of data for economic growth [ 191 , Recitals 2–3], the Copyright Directive preventing restrictions on technological development [ 192 , Recital 3], MiCA focusing broadly on business and employment growth [ 193 , Recitals 1–4], DSA harmonizing rules for responsible provision of online platforms and services across Member States to protect the internal market [ 194 , Recitals 2, 4], as well as the AI Act [ 195 , Recital 4], DMA [ 194 , Recital 1], DO [ 106 , Recitals 1–3], Data Act [ 196 , Recitals 1–5] and Chips Act [ 197 , Recitals 2–4] mentioning improved competitiveness and digital sovereignty. Perhaps unsurprisingly, these predictions tend to be vague or high-level. Specific mechanisms to drive economic growth are rarely discussed beyond affirmations of compliance with the EU's high regulatory standards as a sign of quality (and thus, competitiveness) for tech products and services [ 106 , Recital 2].

Concerning the latter, the AI Act 61 and DGA [ 198 , Recitals 1–5] predict benefits across a wide range of publicly beneficial sectors including healthcare, mobility and sustainability, while the EMFA focuses specifically on opportunities for media such as online offerings and services [ 199 , Recitals 2–7]. These more concrete predictions suggest that legislators see innovation as having clear value for the public, which may justify the subsidies discussed above ( §2 ).

Importantly, the need to balance these predicted benefits with risks to the public and organizations is evident across the reviewed policies. Several frameworks focus on balancing economic growth and competitiveness against protections for specific rights. The GDPR [ 191 , Recitals 2–3] and DGA [ 198 , Recitals 1–5] mention balancing the free flow of data for economic growth with data protection and privacy rights. The Copyright Directive seeks to balance IP rights with technological development [ 192 , Recital 3]. Both the AI Act [ 200 , 201 ] and PLD [ 202 , Recitals 1–5] serve as key consumer protection frameworks to protect the health, safety and other interests of individuals against AI and digital products. The AI Act recognizes specific legal and ethical challenges stemming from bias, opacity, misinformation and environmental sustainability or protection [ 195 , Recitals 27, 61]. 62 The DSA seeks to ensure responsible and diligent provision of online platforms and services while protecting fundamental and individual rights, particularly freedom of expression and non-discrimination [ 194 , Recitals 2–3]. Finally, the PAR echoes this concern with misinformation, focusing on the need to combat voter deception, disinformation and political interference stemming from social media and other digital technologies [ 204 , Recital 4, pp. 7–10].

More generally, the GDPR [ 191 , Recitals 2–3], AI Act [ 195 , Recitals 1, 4–5], DO [ 106 , Recitals 1–2] and EMFA [ 199 , Recitals 2–7] seek a balance between economic growth and technology uptake with fundamental rights and European values broadly conceived. Risks of unfair and distorted competition practices such as lock-in effects, vertical integration and other dependencies feature in both the PLD [ 202 , Recitals 1–5] and DMA, with the latter noting that the economic value created by online platforms and gatekeepers needs to coexist with healthy competition [ 194 , Recital 1].

EU legislators thus envisage a variety of risks to individual rights and public goods such as health, safety, fundamental and individual rights, and consumer protection. At the same time, they believe that innovation will be socially beneficial. Their legislative mandate is to find a balance between these risks and benefits.

EU tech policy is thus defined by risk mitigation. Reflecting this, the reviewed policies rarely place positive obligations on tech providers and deployers unrelated to mitigation of perceived risks, for example new individual rights or positive equality duties for the public sector [ 205 ], [ 206 , p. 727], [ 207 ]. 63 Policy rarely prescribes a positive, proactive vision for emerging technologies and the role they can and should play in society. Instead, it tends to be reactive, 64 seeking to make sense of the novel capabilities of new technologies and their risks, and to create rules to ensure their alignment with fundamental EU rights and values.

AI Act : uses a risk-based approach, where predictive AI systems are categorized according to their predicted level of risk, with different restrictions applying based on degree [ 190 , 200 ], [ 209 , pp. 6–7], [ 210 , pp. 685–686]. Positive obligations, for example to improve education or job satisfaction by deploying AI, are not prescribed. General-purpose AI systems receive similar treatment; specific systemic risks must be mitigated, including discrimination, national security, misinformation and others [ 195 , Recital 110]. Providers and deployers are not, however, required to improve the quality of democracy or national security with AI.

GDPR : uses a risk-based approach [ 211 , 212 ]. Distinguishes between data types based on identifiability and sensitivity to determine their level of riskiness and necessary restrictions on processing. Anonymized data, for example, is lowest risk based on the assumption that a person cannot be re-identified and thus cannot have their privacy violated. Personal data and sensitive personal data warrant comparatively higher degrees of protection [ 191 , Recitals 26, 28, 51, 53, 75–77]. 65 The framework does not stipulate that data controllers must use personal data for socially beneficial purposes; rather, they need only to reduce the risk of privacy harms for individuals.

DSA : the DSA sets out requirements for Very Large Online Platforms and Very Large Online Search Engines based on systemic risks posed to fundamental rights, electoral processes, misinformation, gender-based violence and minors, among others [ 194 , Recitals 1–2, Article 35]. In contrast, the DSA does not impose positive obligations related to these risks, for example, to promote fundamental rights or gender equality, or contribute to the mental well-being of minors.

Product Liability Directive : inherently about risk mitigation as a type of tort law. It ensures recourse and redress for individuals harmed by (AI) products, thereby providing an incentive for providers to reduce risks of harm. It does not, however, stipulate that (AI) products need to be socially beneficial.

Copyright Directive : grants IP rights to creators to protect their work. However, it also creates rules, restrictions and time limits to reduce the risk of IP rights stifling further creation by others. The CD does not require creative works to be socially beneficial. 66

Defining and measuring the societal benefits of innovation is difficult. A ‘common good’ or positive vision of society towards which AI should be designed and used is not explicitly defined by legislators in the reviewed policies. Provisions and requirements meant to protect individual rights and societal interests from the risks posed by new technologies tend to be more concrete and enforceable than predicted benefits. Policies claim that compliance with EU legal requirements act as a mark of quality for tech products and services, giving them a competitive advantage. 67 Further, general affirmations of EU rights, laws and values, as well as references to areas such as healthcare, agriculture, food safety and education suggest a vague conception of common good, but details are lacking about how AI (and other emerging technologies) should concretely benefit the public in these areas. Rather than setting specific goals for innovation to deliver concrete benefits to society, laws tend to leave measurement and delivery of predicted benefits open-ended, underspecified and thus unenforceable. This gap means that, at least from a regulatory perspective, the social benefits of new technologies cannot be guaranteed via risk mitigation alone.

AI poses a fundamental strategic challenge to EU tech policy because its potential applications and risk profiles are so broad. As a technology that can seemingly replace or augment any type of human intellectual labour, reliably predicting the full range of its possible use cases is practically impossible. The same can be said of the risks it poses to individuals, society, fundamental and individual rights and other interests. 68

General-purpose and generative AI's risk profile is exceptionally broad in the sense that the range of potential risks grows in step with its applications across sectors [ 215 ]. Further, many risks are (i) poorly understood, in the sense that their nature, scale, severity or frequency are not matters of scientific consensus, or (ii) poorly regulated, in the sense that current regulatory frameworks are not effective at mitigating them, do not address them at all or fail to address emerging dimensions of the risk in question. 69 Examples of poorly understood or poorly regulated risks of general-purpose and generative AI systems include:

employment and economic inequality : widespread unemployment or displacement owing to automation and uncertain economic mechanisms to replace lost labour and income, downward pressure on wages, work quality, collective bargaining power and job security owing to competition from AI for work, homogeneity in AI-driven recruitment decisions [ 216 , p. 221], [ 217 , pp. 254–255], [ 218 , pp. 641, 648–649], [ 219 ];

technological inequality : unequal access to AI resources for work, education, personal projects and other areas, and unequal burden of costs from its usage [ 181 , 184 , 226 ];

environment and sustainability : under-reporting and gamification of efficiency standards, impact on local and regional environment and residents, competition for scarce resources such as water, electricity and land, degradation of local infrastructure [ 46 , pp. 13–15], [ 203 , p. 148], [ 227–230 ], [ 231 , pp. 612–613];

IP : unauthorized training and copying of creative works, competition for creative work, devaluing of creative work owing to difficulty of separating human from artificially generated works [ 232 , 233 ], [ 234, p. 22], [ 235 ];

public discourse and shared knowledge : hallucinations, careless speech, deepfakes, AI-generated misinformation and disinformation and algorithmic nudges undermining the quality of public discourse, consensus, shared knowledge and the information environment [ 71 , 216 ], [ 236 , pp. 7–8], [ 237 , pp. 1–2, 11–12];

The breadth and severity of these under-regulated or poorly understood AI risks are stark. EU tech policy is comparatively narrow, meaning it focuses on specific sectors, applications or values and rights and their related tangible risks (e.g. non-discrimination, environmental standards and data protection; §4 ), 70 but struggles to effectively manage long-term, holistic and cumulative risks, where the harm is widespread and difficult to measure. 71 As we have already seen, positive visions and obligations are also conspicuously absent.

This situation is unacceptable from the view of policymakers’ mandate to find an appropriate balance between the risks and benefits of new technologies for society. Individuals in the EU are paying substantial subsidies to support AI ( §2 ) and facing poorly understood but wide-ranging risks from its deployment, while only being promised vaguely defined benefits in return ( §3 ). Continuing solely down the pathway of risk mitigation is unsustainable for the future of AI; the costs and risks placed on the public are simply too great, with too little guaranteed in return. Going forward, EU tech policy needs a third goal to rebalance AI governance alongside the goals of ‘risk mitigation’ and ‘economic growth’. We argue that AI providers seeking or currently benefiting from public subsidies should be obligated to provide detailed plans for expected benefits of the technology to individual happiness and social well-being, against which they can later be assessed.

Happiness as a third goal for EU tech policy is justified by two observations. First, AI companies already received many subsidies from and on behalf of the public, in the form of privileged access to resources like land, water, electricity and data; access to public funds and tax breaks; and regulatory leniency and political capture of policy-making processes ( §2 ). These subsidies enable their success on the market but are not given with any guarantees of future societal benefits (but rather only vague promises and predictions by companies and policymakers). Happiness as a policy goal can help to ensure companies actually develop, deploy and govern AI in a way that will concretely benefit the people subsidizing its very existence.

Second, policymakers are obligated to act in the best interests of the public. With AI, they are doing so under conditions of significant uncertainty. The risks discussed above are, if realized, extremely severe and disruptive for society. The predicted benefits are likewise vaguely defined. This raises several questions: why is the only party benefiting from this arrangement AI companies while the other pays the costs? Why are policymakers not compelling companies to concretely define their predicted benefits, and hold them accountable if they do not deliver? The public is in all but name a shareholder of AI companies.

We are not alone in observing the limitations of technology development and policy to deliver promised social benefits. Many initiatives have been founded in recent years to redirect technology development, governance and regulation towards more human-centric, less economic goals. 72 Scholars have also made influential policy proposals, such as Barbara Prainsack and Alexa Buyx's groundbreaking and compelling proposal to use ‘solidarity’ as a policy and governance goal when regulating data access [ 190 , 248 , 249 ], Linnet Taylor's work on ‘data justice’ [ 250 ], or Jack Balkin and Jonathan Zittrain's proposal to classify data processors as information fiduciaries responsible for realizing the best interests of their data subjects [ 251 , 252 ], [ 253 , pp. 339–341].

Further, using happiness as a public policy goal is also not unprecedented, with many countries already using happiness or the broader concept of ‘well-being’ as guiding principles for public policy decision-making balanced with economic growth or GDP (for an overview of approaches, see table 2 and appendix B ). Many of these approaches are based in welfare economics and use theoretical frameworks such as Sen's capabilities approach to operationalize the concept of welfare beyond GDP or market competitiveness [ 254 ]. While none of these national approaches listed below are without flaw, and we do not endorse any of them explicitly, their existence shows that happiness already has traction in various forms within policy-making internationally.

In comparison with these approaches and the broader umbrella of welfare economics, here we choose a narrower focus on antecedents of happiness as described in psychology to provide clear, empirical grounding for the concept to serve as a third goal for EU tech policy. This narrower focus enables us to recommend precise interventions in existing EU tech policy to improve individual happiness and social well-being compared with the broader, societal lens of welfare economics. In the following section, we discuss five decades of psychological research on human happiness to understand its antecedents and value for society. Through a series of policy proposals, we then show how happiness can guide technology development, adoption and governance as a counterweight to risk mitigation.

Happiness is not reducible to attainment or a sense of satisfaction in the sense of obtaining what one wants at any given moment. A person may experience an easy life in ways that are disconnected from others, ineffective in practice, or alien to their own values, but these benefits are not expected to last long [ 255 ]. In addition, a person may feel stress or disappointment while living well in a fuller psychological sense [ 256 ], [ 257 , pp. 150–151], [ 258 , p. 1].

For decades, psychological theories have argued that true happiness is grounded in meaningful engagement in the world [ 258–263 ]. Across these traditions, three antecedents of happiness have received extensive empirical support: these are relatedness, self-efficacy (i.e. competence) and autonomy. Framed as basic psychological needs (e.g. SDT) [ 264 ], or as fundamental aspects of psychological well-being [ 261 , 265 , 266 ], these dimensions are understood to be necessary for defining global well-being and predicting sustained happiness.

The first of these—relatedness—reflects the social nature of human beings, who have evolved such that they are fundamentally motivated to form and maintain lasting interpersonal bonds [ 267 , 268 ]. 73 It is not only that relationships matter, but that they matter in a way that facilitates happiness and well-being. A life cannot be understood to be going well if it is marked by chronic loneliness or alienation, even if it feels pleasurable or comfortable.

At its core, relatedness concerns the experience of being connected to others, cared for by them and caring for them [ 261 , 270 , 271 ]. But relatedness can come in many forms. Relatedness is felt when people feel known, understood and valued, when they experience others as responsive to their needs and perspectives, and when relationships allow for warmth, trust and mutual significance. Research on perceived partner responsiveness, for example, shows that people flourish when they feel that others close to them ‘get’ them, validate them and care about them, suggesting that relatedness is less about the quantity of social connection and more about perceptions of oneself as meaningfully engaged with others [ 272 ].

The links between relatedness and happiness have received strong support from large-scale empirical evidence. For example, a recent global analysis reported in the World Happiness Report synthesized data from 22 countries and regions in the Global Flourishing Study and the Gallup World Poll data. It found that stronger social connection and perceived social support were associated with higher life satisfaction both within and across countries [ 279 ]. Furthermore, young adults who reported at least one close relationship are 16% more satisfied with their lives on average than those who reported no close ties. This global evidence converges with a separate meta-analysis by Holt-Lunstad et al. [ 280 ], which synthesized 148 studies and found that stronger social relationships were associated with lower mortality, or in other words, increased likelihood of survival. Together, these findings suggest that relatedness is not just one desirable feature of a good life, but rather that it is a basic condition of well-being.

Crucially, relatedness is primarily, but not exclusively, a social experience.
