It can also be met through parasocial relationships, including through connection to fictional characters [ 281 ] and God [ 282 , 283 ]. The brunt of evidence in parasocial relatedness concerns nature connection, the feeling that one meaningfully connects to the natural world. Connection to nature is particularly relevant in this context owing to the loss of access to land and other natural resources currently being faced by residents living near data centres ( §2.1 ).

Findings show that among people spending time alone in nature, higher connectedness to nature is associated with less loneliness. In contrast, people feel lonelier when alone in nature but feeling low nature connection [ 284 ]. The evidence concerning loneliness, in particular, suggests that nature connection can act as a substitute for human connection. Earlier work has also found that nearby nature buffered the harmful effects of low social connectedness on subjective well-being, similarly suggesting that nature may partly compensate for deficits in social ties [ 285 ].

Nature connection also appears to matter more broadly for happiness and well-being. Meta-analytic studies report that people who feel more connected to nature report greater positive emotions and life satisfaction [ 286 ]. Studies also show that people who report more nature connection report not only feeling happier, but also broader indicators of psychological well-being, including mindfulness, meaning and a greater sense of aliveness [ 286 , 287 ]. Connection to nature is particularly relevant in this context owing to the loss of access to land and other natural resources currently being faced by residents living near data centres ( §2.1 ).

People are not only social by nature. They are also doers, builders and thinkers. The capacity to act effectively in the world is central to productivity and to happiness [ 288 ]. Competence (also termed self-efficacy) refers to the felt experience that one is able to undertake tasks and achieve goals that are felt to be important: that one can act effectively, meet challenges such that efforts put in really matter, learn, solve problems and bring about meaningful and desired outcomes [ 289 ]. It is a core psychological resource that shapes whether individuals approach demanding situations with confidence or helplessness [ 290 , 291 ]. It is felt when people take on optimal challenges (challenges that stretch them, but which they can successfully complete) [ 292 , pp. 44–46], [ 293 , p. 90], when they do meaningful or interesting work, and when they receive feedback that signifies progress [ 294 , pp. 256–257], [ 295 ].

Competence is understood to be more than a side-benefit of successful actions; rather, it inspires purposeful action [ 288 ]. Research on learned helplessness [ 291 , 296 , 297 ]—the feeling that one's actions are unrelated to meaningful or desired outcomes in the environment—highlights the happiness costs of deficits in competence. People (or, in original research, animals [ 298 ]) feel or act depressed when they are repeatedly exposed to uncontrollable outcomes and start to expect that their actions are not related to meaningful outcomes. In these settings, those who expect non-contingency between actions and outcomes stop trying to act even when change has become possible; in other words, helplessness leaves people unmotivated to exert effort and act on the world. These patterns are core symptoms of depression [ 299 , pp. 230–235]. On the other hand, when people feel competent, they see problems as difficult, but they feel motivated to face challenges [ 300 ]. Across decades of work on the topic, psychologists have shown that beliefs about one's ability to exercise control over events are central to motivation, persistence and adjustment in major life domains ranging from education to work [ 290 , 296 , 297 , 301 ].

People feel happy not when they are presented with no challenges, but rather when they are presented with challenges that feel manageable and worth undertaking. These include better life satisfaction, stronger coping and better adjustment under stress [ 290 , 297 ], [ 302 , p. 60]. At work, experiencing challenging demands is linked to more positive emotions [ 303 , pp. 703–704], so long as they are not excessive and therefore once again undermine competence [ 304 ]. When jobs are restructured, those who feel capable of handling the challenge can meet changes with better psychological well-being, stronger engagement and higher job satisfaction over time [ 305 ].

Meaningful, rather than frivolous, work also supports happiness through competence. When people experience their work as meaningful, growth-promoting and reflecting their capacities, they are more likely to experience well-being ([ 289 ]; see also [ 306 , 307 ]). Research increasingly suggests that such meaningful work is linked to greater happiness across emotional (lower negative emotions), cognitive (better life satisfaction) and physical (i.e. better health) dimensions [ 308 ], including in studies that track people's work habits across time [ 309 ].

Finally, it is now clear from five decades of research that neither ‘relating’ nor ‘doing’ can foster deep feelings that one is ‘related’ or ‘competent’ without also having the characteristic of being ‘autonomous’ [ 263 ]. Autonomy is a fundamentally important, and often misunderstood, driver of happiness. Colloquially, autonomy is often taken to mean independence, self-sufficiency or freedom from the influence of other people; ‘autonomous’ people are assumed to stand apart, resist influence and rely only on themselves. However, this individualistic definition is not how the construct is typically understood in psychology. Researchers understand that one can rely deeply on others and still feel autonomous as in the case of cooperating with doctors’ orders for treatment of a deadly illness, or appear independent while feeling internally controlled as in the case of a hard-working but highly pressured executive whose sense of value as a person depends entirely on his success at work. An SDT conceptualization of autonomy thus differentiates it from both individualism and independence, and in this sense aligns with feminist and indigenous relational-autonomy views, whereby connections with other people, communities and the natural world are not antithetical to autonomy, but rather help to form autonomy-relevant dimensions such as identity, values and self-trust [ 310 , 311 ].

Within SDT and related approaches [ 267 , 312–314 ], autonomy is not understood as separateness or independence per se , but instead as volition: the experience of acting with a sense of willingness and inner valuing rather than pressure or compulsion. From these views, people feel autonomous when their actions are endorsed from within, experienced as their own and carried out with a sense of psychological authorship, that is, with the feeling that ‘this is really coming from me’ rather than being imposed from outside (most often by other people, but possibly, other external forces). Autonomy may be felt when one behaves from deeply held values, because actions are meaningful and important, because actions are rewarding, or because acting fulfils curiosity or interest [ 267 ]. In contrast, autonomy is undermined when actions are driven primarily by compliance, coercion or felt pressure.

Extensive evidence links autonomy to happiness and happiness-related outcomes. For example, cross-cultural work across four to eight countries at a time suggests that well-being is reliably higher when people pursue goals for reasons they can genuinely stand behind, whereas independence is much less predictive of happiness across cultures [ 289 , 315 , 316 ]. In a growing number of studies, social relationships are understood to predict well-being only insofar as they fulfil autonomy. For example, in romantic relationships such as marriages, spouses must support their partners’ autonomy to bring them happiness [ 317 ], [ 318 , p. 452], and even friendships are based on the mutual exchange of autonomy support, with each partner supporting the agency of the other [ 319 , pp. 314–315], [ 320 , 321 ]. Even a behaviour as fundamentally social as helping others (i.e. prosocial behaviours) conduces happiness benefits for both helper and recipient insofar as they are autonomous rather than pressured or coerced [ 322 , 323 ]. Autonomy, on this view, is not opposed to care; rather, it is one of the conditions that makes care psychologically rewarding.

In one of the largest early studies testing autonomy, Tay and Diener analysed Gallup World Poll data from 123 countries and showed that people who had autonomy experienced more positive emotions and were more satisfied with their lives across the world [ 321 , p. 362]. Importantly, within this massive dataset, autonomy was important above and beyond economic factors such as household income. More recent large-scale evidence again points to global happiness benefits of autonomy. Data from the World Values Survey across 66 countries and nearly 100 000 respondents showed that autonomy was associated with more happiness and life satisfaction across the world, and was an even stronger predictor at the national level than nation-level wealth [ 324 , pp. 12–13].

In sum, this work suggests that it is not enough to experience pleasure and economic attainment. Rather, people feel happy when they are connected to others, pursue and progress meaningful challenges and do both volitionally, from a sense of interest and caring. Relatedness is important for happiness because as social creatures, quality connections outside of the self, rather than alienation, is fundamental to living well. Competence is important because we seek to do well, to build and contribute in meaningful ways. Autonomy matters because we need to operate in a way that expresses and is congruent with what is interesting and valuable, and feel little benefit from either connection or accomplishment when it is felt as pressured or imposed.

Having defined antecedents of happiness, we can turn to a fundamental question that determines the need for such definitions: why should policymakers and the AI industry care that the general public is happy?

First, happiness holds intrinsic value for the public as a central way that people evaluate the quality of their lives [ 325 , 326 ]. The same idea has been posited in economics, which has increasingly recognized that people's reports about a ‘worthwhile life’ centrally involve happiness, and therefore, production or consumption metrics are insufficient alone for defining individual success [ 327 ].

This, then, has implications for which benchmarks should be used to identify successful functioning of a society. If society is meant to serve the needs, desires and ambitions of its people, then their own experience of whether life is going well must be considered as an indicator of societal success. Importantly for our purposes, happiness is such an indicator.

But the case for happiness remains strong even if we set aside the point of individual benefits and instead evaluate the utility of happiness as a greater good to society (i.e. social well-being). Happy people are better learners, healthier (and therefore less likely to draw on limited public resources), more productive employees and creative problem-solvers (which can contribute to social progress) and more helpful contributors to a cohesive society.

For example, a large review concluded that happiness is associated with, and often precedes, success across major life domains, including at work [ 328 , pp. 831–832]. Experimental evidence points in the same direction, finding that people who are made happier become more productive in paid tasks [ 329 ], challenging the assumption that people need material success to become happy. These findings indicate that happiness is a driver of other socially desired outcomes rather than an end goal achievable through other means. Further, it suggests that the relationship does not only run from productivity to happiness, but rather runs the other way around as well. Happiness helps to bring about many of the outcomes that governments, legislators and industry leaders already value.

A similar pattern appears in education, wherein happiness is positively associated with academic achievement [ 330 , p. 91] and creative performance [ 331 ], [ 332 , pp. 1875–1879]. The association between happiness and greater creativity matters because creative thought is the foundation for innovation and problem-solving, including for broader economic and societal advancement.

Finally, happiness also matters because it seems to support prosociality and social cohesion. For example, Gallup World Poll data from 163 countries found that happiness was positively associated with giving time and money to others [ 333 , p. 857]. In other words, happier people are not only more satisfied with their own lives, but they also seem more likely to help others. Arguably, happiness creates a positive feedback loop wherein happier people are more prosocial, which in turn makes them happier, and ultimately, more prosocial [ 334 , p. 232]. In all, a society made up of happier people is likely to be productive, cooperative and caring.

The three psychological antecedents of happiness discussed in the previous section (i.e. competence, relatedness and autonomy) are also important for social well-being as well as individual happiness. Specifically, when people feel competent, they are more likely to approach tasks with confidence, persist when difficulties arise and experience themselves as capable of influencing their environment. When people feel related, they are more likely to trust others, invest in relationships, cooperate and remain embedded in the kinds of stable social bonds that support cohesive social life. When people feel autonomy supported, they are more likely to bring genuine effort, interest and commitment to what they do. As such, these needs are the foundation that allows people to learn, work, create, care and participate well in families, schools, workplaces and communities, ultimately leading to stronger and more productive communities [ 264 , 335 ].

Indeed, one reason that we have focused on these three needs in this article is that each supports a different aspect of human behaviour which ultimately contributes to social well-being. Competence helps sustain mastery and persistence, particularly but not solely in the face of challenge. Relatedness builds mutual care and belonging, which in turn support trust and cooperation and ultimately, social coherence. Autonomy energizes action; research shows that people are more engaged when what they do feels self-endorsed [ 336 , p. 1025]. A society that supports these conditions is therefore not only making people feel better. It is also creating the motivational and relational conditions under which people are more likely to contribute and cooperate [ 271 ], [ 336 , p. 1025], [ 337 ].

Current EU tech policy attempts to balance the risks and benefits of emerging technologies measured in terms of economic growth and risks to fundamental and individual rights and EU values ( §4 ). AI industry promotional material likewise focuses predominantly on the economic benefits of their technologies ( §3 ). These dual trends have resulted in a situation where the subsidies offered on behalf of the public to the AI industry are not offering a fair ‘return on investment’ to society. A more promising approach could be to use ‘happiness’ as a policy mandate and metric to evaluate the predicted and actual risks and benefits of innovation.

Psychological research offers empirical evidence about what actually makes people happy ( §5 ). According to SDT, the key antecedents of happiness are relatedness, competence and autonomy. Relatedness refers to the core psychological need of having (social) connections with friends, family, community and nature. Competence refers to the drive to understand, learn, master and use skills to meet meaningful goals. Finally, autonomy refers to a sense of willingness to pursue goals. These three key elements are the foundation for predicting happiness and well-being.

This ‘happiness framework’ can work as a compass for tech policy decisions. Evidence is mounting that emerging tech products and services can harm psychological well-being and happiness. The three antecedents of happiness cast emerging use cases, risks and benefits in a new light that suggests different policy priorities and goals are urgently needed to strike an appropriate balance between growth, public goods and fundamental and individual rights. A few illustrative examples show their value for understanding emerging tech policy challenges.

Competence is highly relevant to risks of deskilling via generative AI. Recent deployments of generative AI across universities and schools may undermine students' educational skills. Evidence is rising that generative AI harms students’ capacities in information retention, 74 performance on mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension tasks [ 222 , 339 ], writing skills [ 340 ], critical thinking [ 341 , p. 15] and creativity [ 342 ]. Similar phenomena can be observed in medicine with deskilling of doctors from the use of AI tools; one study showed, for example, that doctors are less able to detect cancer manually after having used AI tools for only three months [ 343 ]. Cognitive abilities are inherently and instrumentally valuable to society (e.g. having competent lawyers and doctors), but also strong antecedents of happiness. 75

Relatedness is uniquely poised to make sense of the impact of AI chatbots. Companion chatbots for friendships, relationships and grieving are increasingly common [ 344 ]. The current business model—very similar to the attention economy [ 345 , pp. 12–16]—focuses on keeping users engaged for as long as possible [ 71 , 346 , 347 ]. Chatbots that are designed to mimic human emotion and empathy enable parasocial relationships ( §5.1 ), but reduce opportunities for real human and nature connection [ 344 ]. Engagement with chatbots can harm mental health and lead to ‘AI psychosis’ [ 348 ], suicide [ 349–351 ], loneliness, dependence and isolation [ 339 , 352–354 ]. Finally, data centres need natural resources such as land, water and electricity [ 46 , pp. 13–15], [ 203 , 227 , 228 ], and contribute to climate change [ 355 , pp. 2–3]. People living near data centres are losing access to natural land and resources to subsidize their construction and operation, further limiting opportunities for connection to nature [ 356 , p. 22].

Autonomy illuminates the risk of large language models (LLMs) and chatbots turning increasingly sycophantic to keep users engaged and online, as well as other novel forms of persuasion ([ 245 , 357 ]; see also [ 358 ]). Personalized responses can very effectively nudge users, for example to buy products or services [ 359 ]. These trends, as well as decisions to incorporate advertising into generative AI, will probably reduce people's autonomy, or ability to willingly pursue meaningful goals without coercion or undue external influence [ 242 , 360 ].

Policymakers and regulators can use the proposed happiness framework, with its three key elements, to balance societal and industrial interests in future tech policy. It can also help industry and the public make decisions about the development, deployment, adoption and governance of emerging technologies. We propose several concrete suggestions to incorporate these ideas into current tech policy-making, business practices and public adoption.

AI companies currently enjoy significant public subsidies to enable their research and development ( §2 ). When policymakers are deciding whether these privileges should be granted or extended, they should require companies to provide detailed plans describing expected benefits for individual happiness and social well-being. These plans should ideally include design specifications and design choice justifications, specific planned use cases, happiness metrics and scientific evidence underpinning all of the above. Developing specific, binding evidentiary requirements, including, for example, documentary or technical standards, should be the subject of future research and policy development. This work would be ideally carried out by independent bodies or regulators themselves to avoid dilution via lobbying in practice [ 114 , 361 ].

It should be noted that our proposal finds common ground with prior work on public value and innovation, such as Prainsack's notions of data justice and solidarity in the realm of data governance. 76 This can introduce new incentives beyond profitability, thereby encouraging companies to change how they design and deploy new technologies. It likewise provides additional leverage to regulators and the judiciary to demand changes when harmful subsidized products are placed on the market (see below).

Policymakers and regulators have a legal mandate to balance competing interests ( §4 ). The vague promise that AI products and services will be socially beneficial is used to justify lobbying, deregulation and weakening of fundamental and individual rights protections for the sake of innovation. Here, happiness can also serve as a balancing factor within the strong risk mitigation approach taken in EU tech policy. The current approach predominantly takes a narrow focus on reducing risks rather than ensuring concrete, positive impacts from AI products and services. Happiness can create a ‘floor’ for policy-making to ensure AI is socially beneficial, not only less risky. The fact that a technology is less harmful does not mean it is socially beneficial.

When administering penalties, regulators and judges must take individual circumstances into consideration. For example, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) traditionally receive lower fines than multi-national companies. Illegal actions committed with malice or intent are punished more severely than those resulting from negligence. If technologies harm people's happiness measured in terms of relatedness, competence or autonomy, penalties should reflect this fact. Regulators and judges could, for example, require changes to the design of a product to mitigate specific harms to these three antecedents of happiness. AI data centre operators found to have misreported resource usage or environmental impact, for example, could face steeper fines owing to the downstream impact their actions have on residents' access to nature ( §5.1 ).

User empowerment, choice and literacy are important factors in people making decisions about how and to what extent they want to integrate technology into their lives. The three antecedents of happiness can help end users make these difficult decisions. Through public awareness campaigns and knowledge transfer, people can be encouraged to ask themselves questions like: will this technology enable me to make closer social or nature connections? Will it help me to master a new skill, and does it require dependency (e.g. generative AI)? Will it help me form and pursue life goals? Overall, will it make me happier?

The antecedents of happiness can help the AI industry. Relatedness, competence and autonomy can guide how products and services are designed and deployed, and serve as a counterweight to economic incentives and socially harmful business models. Companies should focus more on developing products that promote these three concepts, albeit without taking a simplistic or paternalistic approach (e.g. forcing users of a social networking app to contact friends once a day to improve relatedness). 77 Technologies are, of course, already designed with them in mind, but are often backed by harmful business models or features that outweigh their benefits to happiness. For example, dating and friendship apps enable human connection, digital libraries and online lectures enable learning and mastery of new skills, and health tracking apps enable people to achieve their health or life goals. Each of these examples coexists with socially harmful design choices meant to maximize profit or engagement at the cost of user well-being, such as ‘swiping’ behaviour on dating apps or excessive gamification of health goals.

People often struggle to understand and predict what makes them happy. Offloading cognitive work by using an LLM to write an essay for school may appear immediately beneficial to a stressed student. Connecting with a chatbot to alleviate loneliness might also seem like a good replacement for human connection. However, people require support to make sensible choices in such scenarios that will lead to more fulfilled lives.

Happiness research can provide such support if embedded in school curricula, AI literacy obligations, or similar learning opportunities. Some countries have already invested in this direction; Delhi, India, for example, implemented the Happiness Curriculum in 2018, which focuses on holistic learning aims rather than strictly academic outcomes [ 363 ]. 78 In Germany, a research project at TU Braunschweig advocates for integration of daily ‘happiness lessons’ into the curriculum [ 365 ]. While not a formal subject in school, the UK also urges investments in resources for well-being and mental health for students, and expects schools to cover mental health issues as part of the relationships and sex education and health education curriculum [ 366 ]. Based on our findings, we recommend further rollout of such initiatives with a specific focus on the role of emerging technologies in happiness and how to make sensible decisions about personal use.

These proposals are ambitious and open to future interpretation. Many key questions of implementation, measurement and enforcement are intentionally left open for future work. 79 While fully developing and justifying the necessary evidentiary, policy, organizational and technical requirements to implement and enforce these proposals in practice goes beyond the scope of this article, together they provide an initial direction for future research and policy-making efforts to rebalance EU tech policy in favour of social well-being.

Much like the legend of Perseus, the myth of self-made tech billionaires collapses under closer scrutiny. Whereas Perseus required divine gifts to slay Medusa, modern AI companies benefit from the substantial public subsidies lavished upon them by adoring governments. Perseus smartly honoured his divine patrons in thanks for their assistance, yet the same cannot be said of companies benefiting from the people underwriting the current AI boom. This technology may indeed lead to the unfettered economic growth and efficiency predicted by companies, but its impact on society, individual rights and well-being, employment, the environment and other public goods remains far more uncertain and looks increasingly harmful. The public seems to be left blindly subsidizing an international AI ‘arms race’ which will, at best, indirectly benefit them, and at worst actively harm them. Just like the heroes of ancient Greece, AI companies should fear losing ‘divine’ favour if their benefactors feel they have been taken for granted.

The public is in all but name a shareholder of AI companies. 80 To re-establish an appropriate balance between economic and social benefits in EU tech policy, we have proposed a new mandate and metric: happiness. Our proposal is an attempt to rebalance the focus of regulators from predominantly economic considerations towards a more holistic idea of societal progress. Being happy is a goal in itself, but happy people are also good for society. Happiness allows people to learn, work, create, care and participate well in families, schools, workplaces and communities. They are better learners, employees, problem-solvers, more helpful people and better able to build strong social relationships [ 328 , p. 825]. Happiness is a driver of many of the outcomes that governments, legislators and industry leaders already value.

Policymakers should increasingly prioritize relatedness, competence and autonomy as antecedents of happiness to ensure that public support goes to innovation that genuinely improves human happiness and well-being. These goals can be equally beneficial for companies and users themselves, helping guide better decisions which deliver economic and social benefits in tandem, rather than at the expense of one another. Making technology less harmful does not mean it is socially beneficial on balance. The AI industry must be compelled to aim higher, to actively enhance human well-being and fundamental and individual rights with innovation, rather than merely erode them less than originally projected.

However, we observe that the most pressing risks are posed by companies developing, deploying and providing key infrastructure for generative and frontier AI. Throughout this article, we discuss individual and societal interests on the one hand, and economic interests on the other. We interpret these categories through the lens of the EU tech policies reviewed in §4 , which are underpinned by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights among other foundational frameworks. It is in this sense that we use these categories. We do not examine or intend to make categorical claims about the overlap and causal relations between these types of interests, as doing so goes beyond the scope of the article. For readers interested in this area, we would refer them to the brief discussion in §3.3 and related works by economists such as Adam Smith and Karl Polanyi.

Adam Smith, considered by many to be the ‘father’ of capitalism, already recognized this tension in the 18th century. He understood happiness as ‘tranquillity and enjoyment’, and argued that ‘disorders of human life…arise from over-rating the difference between one permanent situation and another’, meaning that the pursuit of improvements to a society's standard of living can undermine its residents’ happiness. See [ 168 , p. 149], [ 169 , p. 310], [ 170 , p. 71], [ 171–173 ].

Adam Smith, for example, observed that as soon as such key basic goods are guaranteed with sufficient wealth (including throughout old age), acquiring more wealth for its own sake should be avoided. Rather, he advises people to focus on the enjoyment of leisurely time and tranquillity [ 168 , 169 , p. 310], [ 170 , p. 9]. Other influential theorists acknowledge the tension between growth and happiness, and warn against the dangers of unfettered economic growth. John Stuart Mill, John Maynard Keynes and John Rawls agree that after a certain living standard is achieved, other pursuits should be prioritized over economic growth. Unfettered growth compromises happiness, leisurely time and justice. See [ 177 , pp. 478–479].

Joseph Stiglitz, for example, has observed that rapid economic growth in the USA in recent decades has predominantly benefited the rich, with the ‘average’ American financially worse off and earning less in real terms than 60 years ago. See [ 178 ]. Policies on education, minimum wage, more stringent tax systems, workers’ rights and anti-discrimination laws are necessary to prevent inequality and increase the welfare of the public. See [ 167 , p. 147]. Thomas Piketty has similarly examined how unfettered economic growth leads to wealth concentration; see [ 166 , p. 25]. More recently, these phenomena have been referred to as the ‘K-shaped’ US economy, with a privileged few responsible for an increasing proportion of spending despite the ‘average’ person being worse off in terms of disposable income. See [ 179 , 180 ].

Adam Smith advocated for a ‘sufficientarian’ standard rather than an egalitarian one, observing that ‘no society can surely be flourishing and happy, of which the far greater part of the members are poor and miserable’. See [ 185 , p. 78]. Modern economists have picked up and reinforced the importance of reducing inequality as an enabler of economic growth. See [ 169 , pp. 315–317], [ 186 , pp. 54–55], [ 187 , pp. 39–41].

Research papers, technical reports, research blog posts and policy white papers were treated as out of scope except where explicitly used for sales or promotional purposes to ensure a narrow focus on promotional materials targeted at potential customers and policymakers. Documents were identified through manual searching of company websites. We reviewed documents published or sponsored by IBM, Google, DeepMind, Microsoft, OpenAI, Amazon Web Services, Nvidia and Anthropic. For each document, we describe its vision for AI (i.e. near- and long-term predictions about the value of generative AI), strategies for implementation and usage (e.g. advice, best practices and insights about generative AI to fulfil aims and objectives) and beneficial use cases.

With regard to vision, most of the reviewed documents describe a vision of generative AI focused on the return on investment and gaining competitive advantages. Described motivations include increasing financial returns, ensuring AI leadership and finding new ways to scale or speed up processes and improve efficiency. None of the reviewed reports focuses on longer-term predictions or visions for AI, with the exception of one document published by Google Cloud [ 122 ].

With regard to strategies, most focus on adoption of AI by a business or organization for optimizing or automating processes, or upskilling where success rate can be measured empirically (e.g. claims regarding process efficiency and faster deployment of new technologies). Comparisons are drawn between ML and generative AI ‘innovations’ focused on improved task efficiency, such as data analysis or document processing. Little attention is given to the reliability or social, ethical or legal factors of AI systems in sales materials, which may instead be dealt with predominantly in research, technical reports and policy white papers. 81

With regard to use cases, the absence of descriptions of concrete, socially beneficial use cases in most of the reviewed promotional materials was notable. They lacked clear descriptions of mechanisms by which predicted social benefits will be delivered (i.e. more than ‘economic growth’, ‘competitiveness’ or ‘efficiency’ as being inherently good). One notable exception is a list maintained by Google Cloud which as of 22 April 2026 lists 1302 use cases of generative AI by organizations worldwide; however, even here concrete details of social benefits are lacking, with each use case receiving a one- to two-sentence description. 82 The focus was instead on high-level descriptions of types of tasks or work that might support specific outcomes (e.g. automated document summarization to increases employee productivity). Across these higher-level descriptions, AI was said to improve customer satisfaction and interactions, employee productivity and efficiency of work processes.

Although unfamiliar to many, ‘happiness’ and related concepts like ‘well-being’ already serve as guiding principles for public policy decision-making in many countries, balanced with economic growth or GDP. None of these examples can be categorically endorsed as the ‘correct’ approach to mandating happiness as a public policy goal owing to vagueness, controversies, implementation challenges, methodological criticisms and other flaws; for example, some approaches reductively equate happiness and well-being with economic growth. Nonetheless, their existence shows that the concept has some traction within policy-making internationally as a foil to a myopic focus on economic growth and GDP.

Policy mandates to measure and improve well-being or happiness have been adopted in several countries. Perhaps the best-known case of a public policy happiness mandate comes from Bhutan. Happiness is explicitly measured through the Gross National Happiness (GNH) index, defined by nine happiness measures (or ‘bowls’) [ 367 ], 83 which are further operationalized via 33 indicators [ 367 ]. 84 An individual is considered happy if they possess at least 66% in all the 33 weighted indicators and ‘bowls’ [ 369 , p. 1]. 85 Bhutan conducts surveys every 3–5 years to assess these measures and indicators. Survey results help guide public policy decisions, the allocation of resources and aim to incentivize NGOs and businesses to focus more on happiness and well-being rather than purely economic growth [ 367 ].

Following Bhutan's shift from an absolute monarchy to a democratic constitutional monarchy, many policies and laws informed by these happiness measures have been introduced from 2008 onwards [ 368 , pp. 492–493, 504]. For example, GNH measures are clearly reflected in Bhutan's current 5-year public policy plan, which prioritizes climate resilience, vocational training, education, healthcare, digital transformation, resilience and governance [ 370 , pp. 4–7]. Their national AI strategy similarly shows influence from the GNH, focusing on ‘holistic wellbeing, sustainability and cultural preservation’ among other goals [ 371 , p. 7]. This holistic approach (‘GNH centric design’) prioritizes AI in key areas like agriculture, tourism and energy, health, education and public services, natural resources and biodiversity, culture and language [ 371 , p. 8].

Other countries have adopted similar mandates, but under the heading of ‘well-being’. A 2009 report by the Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Commission on ‘the limits of GDP as an indicator of economic performance and social progress’ influenced several countries’ approaches to measuring and mandating improvements to well-being. The report advocates for the inclusion of universal ‘quality of life’ measures when assessing social progress [ 372 ]. 86

In 2017, Italy became the first OECD country to explicitly include considerations of well-being and happiness alongside economic considerations when taking public policy and budgetary decisions [ 374 , p. 3]. Italy adapted the report's recommended universal measures into 12 indicators of well-being ( table 2 ), 87 which can be revised over time [ 374 , p. 12].

In 2021, Ireland similarly developed a ‘Well-being Framework’ inspired by the Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Commission, with 11 indicators measured ( table 2 ) every 4–5 years [ 373 ], [ 376 , p. 3], [ 377 ]. 88 Policymakers are directed to factor results into their decisions. Example affected policy measures include a carbon tax, 89 revisions to the tax and welfare system and equality measures (e.g. around gender and age) [ 376 , p. V].

Other approaches draw a simpler direct connection between well-being and economic considerations. For example, in 2019, New Zealand introduced a ‘Wellbeing Budget’ focusing on domestic challenges including mental health, domestic violence and child poverty, support for Māori and Pacific people (e.g. skills and income), digital transformation and productivity, and low-emissions business transformation [ 378 , p. 6]. In 2025, the Public Finance Act 1989 was then amended to require ‘social, economic, environmental and cultural’ well-being considerations to be included in budgetary decision-making [ 379 , para. 26 M]. The improvement of living standards (e.g. health, education, good working conditions, cultural protection, leisure time, friends and family, housing, environmental protection, firms and markets, and good governance) is also linked to ‘well-being’ and ought to guide policy and budgetary decisions [ 380 ]. Nepal has also mandated improved well-being in economic terms via its ‘Prosperous Nepal, Happy Nepali’ plan, which aims to make Nepal a high-income country by 2043. Nepal does not granularly measure happiness, but instead defines it broadly as the realization of higher living standards (e.g. higher income, better healthcare and education, physical infrastructure) and socialist values [ 381 , pp. 4–5, 25].

It is worth remembering that, as discussed above ( §5.3 ), economic considerations are relevant antecedents of happiness, for example, in relation to fulfilment of basic needs, but only to the point of diminishing returns. Further, they are not as strong predictors as other concepts like relatedness, competence and autonomy.

In some countries, well-being and happiness are measured solely for informational and guidance purposes, rather than as part of a public policy mandate. OECD member states, for example, participate in the ‘OECD Well-being Framework’, which compares well-being between countries over time based on measurements across 11 dimensions ( table 2 ) [ 382 , 383 ]. OECD countries do sometimes integrate well-being measurements into policy and budgetary processes, but not owing to a legal mandate [ 374 , p. 14], [ 376 , p. 3].

Similarly, the United Kingdom Office for National Statistics started collecting ‘well-being’ data in 2010 across 10 dimensions and 60 indicators ( table 2 ). 90 The well-being data are intended to inform policymakers and help make decisions, understand the impact of certain actions (e.g. building a new airport) [ 386 ], and otherwise guide the Treasury [ 384 ]. However, unlike Italy and Ireland, policymakers are not legally mandated to use the data to improve societal well-being; rather, it serves as guidance or a checklist to assess competing economic and well-being interests in a fair manner (e.g. the value of a measure and its cost) [ 387 ].

This section does not claim to offer a comprehensive picture or assessment of the efficacy of these public policy ‘happiness’ and ‘well-being’ strategies. 91 However, we have shown that happiness as a public policy compass is not a completely foreign concept. We have surveyed a range of approaches to measure and improve the well-being of the public, ranging from policies that are inspired by religious values and connection with nature to relationships with people and opportunities for choiceful living. These must, of course, be evaluated alongside the concrete social problems facing regions, economic well-being indicators and the improvement of living standards and quality of life. The concepts of relatedness, competence and autonomy are self-evidently reflected, if not explicitly mentioned, in many of these general social policies. 92
